title: I Have Loved You
sum: Malachi opens with a statement of love and an objection. The LORD says, "I love you," and the people ask, "How?" The answer is a comparison with Esau's family: two brothers, two countries, and one of them is now a wasteland. Edom says it will rebuild, but the LORD says whatever it builds he will tear down. The people will see this and say that the LORD is great beyond Israel's border.

The rest of the chapter turns on the priests, the men who run the altar for a small Persian province. They bring blind, lame and stolen animals to the altar and call the LORD's table something to look down on. The LORD asks them to offer the same animals to their governor. He says he wants the doors shut, because no offering from their hands pleases him, and he sets his name, great among the nations and honored by incense and a pure offering everywhere, against the temple's empty ritual.
readings: Read as a courtroom dispute

The six exchanges in the book are shaped like a lawsuit between the LORD and his people: charge, denial, proof and verdict. Chapter 1 gives the first two. The proof for love is Edom's ruin; the proof for contempt is the animals on the altar. This is the covenant-lawsuit pattern of earlier prophets, with the people's own words quoted back to them.
Read as a teaching conversation

Some scholars hear a teacher answering real questions in a community that had stopped expecting much from God. On this reading the 'But you say' lines are the usual doubts of the day, and Malachi's job is to answer them one by one with the covenant.
Read as a message about the nations

1:11 and 1:14 say the LORD's name is great, and feared, among the nations. The chapter sets a small, discouraged community and its poor sacrifices against that large claim, and asks which one is the real picture of God.

views.H: The setting is the Persian province of Yehud after 515 BC. The Temple stands but the community is poor; a governor (1:8) collects gifts; Edom's land is ruined (1:3-4), a fact many link with Arab pressure in the 6th and 5th centuries BC. The cult Malachi describes, with a priesthood receiving animal offerings under the law of Leviticus 22, matches the system of Ezra and Nehemiah. Nehemiah 13:4-9 shows priests misusing Temple rooms in the same decades.
views.C: The book's form is a disputation; the title is 'oracle' (massa'), as in Zechariah 9 and 12; whether 'Malachi' is a name or the word 'my messenger' is disputed. Scholars ask whether 1:2-5 is a separate unit, whether 1:11 is a statement of the present or the future, and whether 'priests' and 'Levi' are one group or two. 1:11 is also one of the hardest verses to date: Persian-period, or a later hope.
views.J: Malachi 1:1-2:7 is the traditional haftarah for Parashat Toledot, the Torah reading where Jacob and Esau are born (Genesis 25:19-28:9), so the Jacob and Esau of Genesis and of Malachi are read side by side. Rashi gives two readings of 1:11. The first, from the Talmud (Menachot 110a), takes it of the nations, who even in worshiping idols know the God over all gods. The second, from the Sages and the Targum Jonathan, takes the pure offering to be Torah study of the Temple laws, and Israel's prayer in every place. Later Jewish writers often use 'Edom' for Rome.
views.X: Paul quotes 1:2-3 in Romans 9:13 to argue about God's free choice. The early church read 1:10-11 of the Eucharist, which it called the pure offering of the nations: the Didache, Justin and Irenaeus say so, and the Council of Trent and the Catechism of the Catholic Church cite 1:11 for the Mass. Reformation churches read the verse of worship and prayer among the nations. See the two cards.

deep.b: The Pentateuch separates priests (the descendants of Aaron) from the Levites who help them. Ezra and Nehemiah keep the distinction. Malachi talks about 'priests' (1:6; 2:1) and then about 'Levi' (2:4-8; 3:3), as if they were the same. Deuteronomy does likewise, speaking of 'the Levite priests' (Deuteronomy 17:9, 18; 18:1). Julia O'Brien argued that Malachi reflects the Deuteronomic idea in which all Levites are priests, and not a quarrel between priests and Levites. Others see the book as a conflict inside the Temple's staff, with the Levites squeezed out (Nehemiah 13:10). The Plain keeps the book's words and lets the reader see the two names.

The nations unknowingly worship the LORD. Rashi's first comment, from Menachot 110a. Israel's own prayer and Torah study. Rashi's second comment, from the Sages, with the Targum Jonathan's paraphrase. Diaspora Jews worship him. Jewish communities such as Elephantine had their own altar by the 5th century BC. A future time. Isaiah 66:18-21 and Zephaniah 3:9-10 expect the nations to bring gifts. The Christian offering. From the Didache to Trent, the Eucharist, a reading the Latin Vulgate's wording ('a sacrifice is made and an offering presented') helps; for the Reformers, the church's worship of prayer and praise. The Hebrew supports more than one of these: it has no verb of time, only two participles, 'is being burned, is being presented'. The Plain keeps the participles and leaves the choice to the reader.

echoes: Genesis 25:19-34; Genesis 27; Deuteronomy 7:7-8; Deuteronomy 23:7; Leviticus 22:17-25; Isaiah 1:11-14; Obadiah 1:10-18; Haggai 2:11-13; Nehemiah 13:4-9; Romans 9:10-13; Didache 14:1-3; Hebrews 13:15; Revelation 8:3-4

settings.what: The oracle of the LORD's love and Edom's ruin
settings.to: The people of the Persian province of Judah (Yehud), the community around the rebuilt Temple in Jerusalem, whom the book calls 'Israel'
settings.when: After the Temple was finished in 515 BC, in the Persian period. The exact date is argued, between about 500 and 430 BC
settings.why: To answer a doubt. A small, poor community under foreign rule asks whether God loves them. The answer is two brothers' histories: Jacob's descendants are back in their land, and Edom's country is a waste. Knowing this makes the verse about the fate of nations and their land, and not about the eternal destiny of two men.
settings.readers: The same first readers: the people addressed are the book's readers, since the book was shaped for the community it names.
views: Most commentators place 1:2-5 after a decline of Edom, perhaps by Arab pressure, and before or near the time of Nehemiah.
A message in the wake of 586
Some read the passage with Obadiah and Lamentations 4:21-22: the Edom of 586 BC and its hope of rebuilding, with Malachi giving the verdict.

settings.to: The priests of the Jerusalem Temple, the men who offered the daily and festival offerings and taught the people the law of clean and unclean
settings.when: In the Persian period, when the Temple was running again and the priests were receiving the people's animals (1:7-8, 1:13-14)
settings.why: To confront priests who accepted bad animals and taught carelessly. The argument is from honor (a son honors a father), from comparison (offer it to your governor) and from the covenant with Levi, a model of what a priest should be (2:5-7). The warning is that the LORD will curse their blessings and make them despised. Knowing the audience shows that the book does not condemn the Temple; it asks the priests to do their work.
views: Some see a conflict between priestly groups, with Malachi on the side of the Levites. O'Brien examines this view and argues against it.
A call to reform of a single order
Others read it as a general complaint of the neglect that Nehemiah 13:4-13 also reports, with no sides.

traditions.q: How do the churches read Malachi 1:2-3, 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated', and Paul's use of it in Romans 9:13?
views: Aquinas (a Thomist reading, one school of Catholic thought and not the whole Church) cites Malachi 1:2-3 in his discussion of God's love and of reprobation, and reads 'hatred' in God as not willing a person the greater good (Summa Theologiae I, q. 20, a. 2; q. 23, a. 3). The Catechism (1037) says God 'predestines no one to go to hell'; it does not discuss Malachi 1:2-3.

The Confession of Dositheus (1672, Decree 3) teaches that God predestines and rejects on the ground of his foreknowledge of how people will respond, and not by compulsion or without cause. It is the Orthodox confession's frame for reading Romans 9; it does not comment on Malachi 1:2-3 itself.

The Formula of Concord (Article XI) teaches election 'in Christ' to salvation for those who believe, and rejects the teaching that God has predestined anyone to damnation. It is a statement about election in general, not a comment on Malachi 1:2-3.

Calvin read Malachi 1:2-3 with Romans 9 as showing that God's love for Jacob rested on his own choice and not on Jacob's worth; the Canons of Dort (chapter 1) teach election and reprobation, with reprobation resting on God's decision to leave some in their sin.

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article V) describes election as God's gracious purpose, consistent with human free agency; it does not mention Malachi. Baptists divide: Calvinist Baptists read Romans 9:13 much as the Reformed do, and others read it of nations and the roles God gave them.

John Wesley rejected unconditional election in sermons such as 'Free Grace' and held that God's election rests on foreknowledge of faith; he read Esau and Jacob in Malachi and Romans 9 as peoples and the privileges given to them, not as an eternal decree for individuals.

traditions.q: Is the 'pure offering' of Malachi 1:11 the Eucharist?
views: Yes: the Council of Trent (Session 22, chapter 1) teaches that the Mass is the clean offering foretold by Malachi to be offered everywhere, and the Catechism cites 1:11 (1350). The Didache, Justin and Irenaeus are read as early witnesses.

The fathers (Didache, Justin, Irenaeus) read the verse of the Eucharist, and the Orthodox liturgy speaks of the 'bloodless sacrifice'; the Confession of Dositheus (Decree 17) teaches that the Eucharist is truly Christ's body and blood, offered in the liturgy. The Orthodox do not define the sacrifice in the scholastic terms of Trent.

The Apology of the Augsburg Confession (Article XXIV) answers that the pure offering is the whole worship of the New Testament, the sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving, and that the Mass is not a sacrifice that earns forgiveness; Lutherans call the Supper a sacrament, a gift to be received.

Calvin read Malachi 1:11 as a prophecy that true worship (prayer, praise, the offering of oneself) would spread among the nations, spoken in the language of the old sacrifices; he rejected the Mass as a sacrifice (Institutes 4.18).

The Lord's Supper is an ordinance, a symbolic memorial of Christ's death, not a repeated sacrifice (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article VII). Malachi 1:11 is usually read of the spread of true worship among the nations.

title: Faithless Priests, Faithless Husbands
sum: The chapter finishes the charge against the priests with the covenant of Levi: life and peace, true teaching, a man who turned many from guilt. The priests have turned aside, so the LORD has made them despised. Then Malachi turns to the community. One father, one God, so why does each man betray his brother? Judah has profaned what is holy to the LORD and married the daughter of a foreign god. Altars are wet with tears, and the LORD has stood as witness between a man and the wife of his youth.

Verses 15 and 16 are the hardest in the book, and the Plain follows the Hebrew word for word. They say the LORD hates sending away, or, in other readings, that a man who hates may send away. The chapter ends with a complaint from the people: 'Where is the God of justice?' Chapter 3 answers it.
readings: Read as two sins: foreign marriage and divorce

Many scholars read 2:10-16 as one scandal: Judean men divorced Judean wives and married women who worshiped other gods. The 'daughter of a foreign god' is a literal woman, and the 'wife of your youth' a literal wife. Verse 16 then forbids sending away a wife for this purpose.
Read as a picture of idolatry

Others take the marriage language as metaphor: Judah has 'married' a foreign god, and the 'wife of your youth' is the covenant itself or the nation. The sin is betrayal of the LORD, and the whole passage is about faith and not marriage.
Read as a general ethic of marriage
A third group reads 2:13-16 as a statement about the marriage covenant that holds in itself, whatever caused it. Jesus's teaching in Matthew 19:3-9 and Mark 10:2-12 is read as taking the same line.

views.H: The Persian-period problem of mixed marriage is documented in Ezra 9-10 and Nehemiah 13:23-27, where the remedy is to send foreign wives away. Malachi 2:16, if it says the LORD hates divorce, may stand against that remedy, or against divorce of Judean wives whatever the context. The date relative to Ezra and Nehemiah is argued. The tears at the altar (2:13) belong to a Temple that still functions.
views.C: Some scholars take 2:11-12 as a later addition or gloss, since they speak of Judah and 'the tents of Jacob' in a way the rest of the passage does not. 2:15 is garbled and perhaps beyond repair; 2:16 has a full variant (the Hebrew, the Greek, the Vulgate and the first words of 4QXIIa); the scroll's visible words agree with the Greek and Latin only in the first clause, and how far the Greek supports a divorce reading is disputed (Fuller, DJD XV and JBL 1991). The chapter shows the book's disputation style at its most tangled, with the speaker moving between God and the prophet.
views.J: The Talmud (Gittin 90a-b) discusses 2:16 as a dispute between 'if you hate, send away' and 'the LORD hates sending away', and says that even the altar sheds tears over a man who divorces his first wife. Rashi and the Targum Jonathan both read 2:16 as 'if you hate her, send her away', a permission with a warning, and Rashi sends the reader to the dispute in Gittin 90b; the reading 'God hates divorce' is the other side of that dispute and a common modern reading. On 2:15 Rashi, following the Targum, takes 'the one' to be the husband who looks for grounds against his wife, who is 'seed of God'; he then adds a story in which the one is Abraham, who sought godly offspring.
views.X: Jesus on divorce (Matthew 19:3-9; Mark 10:2-12) is often read with Malachi 2:14-16, and Christian preachers have used 2:7 for the duty of ministers to teach. The churches differ on what follows for divorce and remarriage; see the card.

deep.h: The verse nobody can fully translate (2:15)
deep.b: Every word of 2:15 has been disputed, from 'one' (echad) to 'a remnant of spirit' (she'ar ruach) to 'offspring of God' (zera' Elohim). The text may be corrupt, or a very compressed argument. The Plain translates the Hebrew words and does not choose a sentence for them. The commentators group into those who find in the verse Genesis 2:24 (God made man and woman one flesh), those who find Abraham (the one father), and those who despair of the Hebrew and follow the Greek. A scroll and the Greek share one change, 'And you say', which makes the question the people's.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the word 'betray' links the marriage verses to the covenant
deep.b: My reading is that the five uses of bagad ('betray') in 2:10-16 are meant to merge the two subjects: betraying a brother (2:10), the LORD's holy place (2:11), a wife (2:14), and one's own spirit (2:15-16). If the hearers feel one sin in these, the passage does not have to be only about foreign marriage or only about divorce; it is about every betrayal inside the household of faith, with marriage as the clearest example. This overlaps with scholars who read the passage as a covenant text (Hugenberger), but the claim that the repeated verb is the author's own bridge is mine.

echoes: Genesis 2:24; Deuteronomy 24:1-4; Numbers 25:10-13; Nehemiah 13:23-29; Ezra 9:1-2; Ezra 10:3; Matthew 19:3-9; Mark 10:2-12; Habakkuk 1:2-4; Jeremiah 12:1

settings.what: The charge of betrayal in marriage and covenant
settings.to: The men of Judah, heads of households in the community, who stood to lose or gain by their marriages; the wives are addressed in the third person
settings.when: In the Persian period, when mixed marriage and divorce were live questions (Ezra 9-10; Nehemiah 13:23-27)
settings.why: To say that how a man treats his wife and his fellow Judeans is a matter of covenant faith, and that the LORD sees it. The altar they use is wet with tears, and he will not accept offerings from men who have wronged their wives. Knowing the audience shows that the passage is a charge to men who held the power to send a wife away, and that its concern is both the wife's wrong and the community's loyalty.
views: Foreign marriage with divorce of Judean wives
The wives betrayed were Judeans, and the men married women who worshiped other gods. This is the commonest view.
Betrayal of the LORD pictured as marriage
Judah's covenant breach, pictured as taking a foreign god's daughter.
The principal charge is the breaking of marriage vows; foreign marriage is a side issue.

settings.what: The people's complaint about justice, and the LORD's answer
settings.to: The community of Judah who say that evildoers prosper in God's eyes and ask where the God of justice is; the answer names the Levites (3:3) and the sinners of 3:5
settings.why: To say that the God of justice is coming, and that those who ask for him should be ready. The charge turns the people's challenge back on them: the one they seek will first purify the Temple's own staff, and then judge sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, those who cheat workers and those who wrong the vulnerable. The answer to 'Where is the God of justice?' is not an excuse but a promise of a visit.
views: A message of judgment on the community
The day will fall on the people who asked, not on foreigners.
The coming is the answer to their prayer; the pain of the passage is that justice cannot be selective.

traditions.q: How do the churches use Malachi 2:16, given that translations disagree on whether it forbids or permits divorce? (Jesus's own answer, in Matthew 19:4-8, goes to Genesis 2:24 and Deuteronomy 24, not to Malachi.)
views: The Latin Church's own Bible reads the verse as a permission: Jerome's Vulgate has 'when you hate her, send her away', and the Douay-Rheims, made from it, follows. Modern Catholic translations such as the New American Bible read 'I hate divorce'. The Church's teaching that a valid, completed marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power (Catechism 1640; Code of Canon Law canon 1141) rests on Matthew 19:3-9 and Genesis 2:24. Spouses may separate (Catechism 1649), and a tribunal can declare that a marriage was never valid.

Marriage is a sacrament meant for life, but the Church allows remarriage after divorce as an act of pastoral mercy (economy), with a penitential service. The question is argued from Matthew 19:9 and the canons, not from Malachi 2:16.

Luther held that marriage is a God-given worldly estate, and that Scripture permits divorce for adultery and for desertion (Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15), with the innocent party free to remarry. His Estate of Marriage does not rest this on Malachi 2:16.

The Westminster Confession (24.5-6) names adultery and willful desertion that the church cannot remedy as grounds for divorce, with the innocent party free to remarry. It does not cite Malachi; many Reformed teachers read 2:16 as 'God hates divorce' and a warning against divorce on other grounds, and others follow the 'if you hate her' reading.

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article XVIII) defines marriage as a lifetime covenant of one man and one woman; it does not cite Malachi or fix the grounds for divorce, and Baptist churches differ on whether divorce is allowed beyond adultery or desertion and on remarriage, including for pastors.

title: The Messenger Comes
sum: The people asked, "Where is the God of justice?" Now the LORD answers: he is sending a messenger to clear the road, and then the Lord they are looking for will come to his temple. Who can live through that day? He is like a refiner's fire and like laundry soap. He will cleanse the descendants of Levi first, and then Judah's offerings will please him as they did long ago. He will also come near to judge the sorcerers, the adulterers, those who lie under oath, and those who cheat workers or push aside widows, orphans and foreigners.

Then the LORD turns to the people's own record. He does not change, but they keep turning aside, so he calls them back: "Return to me, and I will return to you." The test is the tithe and the contribution. Bring the whole tithe to the storehouse, and see whether he will open the sky. The chapter ends in a scene of talk: some say serving God is pointless, and those who fear him speak with each other, and a scroll of remembrance is written for them.
readings: Read as the answer to 2:17

3:1-5 answers 'Where is the God of justice?' with the visit that the people had asked for. In this reading the whole chapter is one movement: the coming (3:1-5), the call to return (3:6-12), and the sorting of the faithful from the proud (3:13-18).
Read as a call to covenant obedience

3:6-12 is the book's plainest call to act: the tithe is the sign that the nation's loyalty is real. The blessing that follows (rain, harvest, no crop pest) is the covenant blessing of Deuteronomy 28:1-14, not a general rule of wealth.
Read as a word for a faithful remnant

3:16-18 shows a small group inside Israel who fear the LORD and talk together. Their scroll of remembrance and 'private treasure' make them the book's remnant, who are told the difference between the righteous and the wicked will again be seen.

views.H: The Temple's storehouse, the tithe and the Levites' shares are the same issues Nehemiah faced in his second term (Nehemiah 13:10-13), so many place Malachi near it. The 'messenger' and the visit to the temple fit the hopes the Persian-period prophets, from Haggai to Zechariah, had for the Temple. The drought and blight echo Haggai 1:10-11 and 2:16-17.
views.C: The identity of the messenger and the messenger of the covenant is the main puzzle (1, 2 or 3 figures). Some scholars think 3:1b-4 is a later insertion, since 3:5 returns to the earlier theme of justice. 3:8-9 has a Greek variant ('trip up') and a very different Greek text of 3:9-10. 3:16-18 is often seen as the book's turn toward a faithful remnant.
views.J: The Haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol, the Sabbath before Passover, is Malachi 3:4-24 (Hebrew), joining the offerings of 3:4 with the coming of Elijah. Jewish commentators read the messenger of 3:1 as Elijah (4:5) or as an angel, and Jewish teachers have read 3:10 as the one place where a person may put God to the test, in giving the tithe.
views.X: Matthew 11:10, Mark 1:2 and Luke 7:27 apply 3:1 to John the Baptist as the messenger who clears the road for Jesus. The Presentation of the Lord (2 February) and the second Sunday of Advent in the lectionaries read 3:1-4; the refiner's fire is a frequent image for the cleansing of the church and of the Christian life (Handel's Messiah is the best-known reception). Tithing churches use 3:8-10; the card shows where the churches differ.
views.F: Futurist readers hold that 3:1-5 is not yet fulfilled in full: the Lord's sudden coming to his temple and the cleansing of Levi are still to come, either at the Second Coming (many Christians) or at the coming of the Messiah (Jewish tradition). Dispensationalists often link the passage with a rebuilt temple. Some preterist and amillennial readers hold that the coming of Christ to the Temple (Luke 2:22-38; Matthew 21:12-13) fulfilled it.

deep.h: The tithe in the law, in Nehemiah and in Malachi
deep.b: The Torah has several laws on the tenth: a tenth of the land's produce belongs to the LORD and is given to the Levites (Leviticus 27:30-33; Numbers 18:21-24); the Levites give a tenth of that to the priests (Numbers 18:25-32); the people eat a tithe at the sanctuary, and every third year leave it for the Levites and the poor (Deuteronomy 14:22-29). Nehemiah says the people promised to bring the tithe to the storerooms (Nehemiah 10:37-39) and that it failed (Nehemiah 13:10-13). Malachi's 'storehouse' and the 'contribution' fit that background. The point is the community's support for the Temple and its servants, not a claim about private wealth.

deep.h: The messenger of the covenant and the Gospels
deep.b: The New Testament takes 3:1 to mean John the Baptist. Jesus says: "It is about him that it is written: 'Look, I am sending my messenger before your face. He will make your road ready ahead of you.'" (Matthew 11:10). Mark begins his Gospel with the same words (Mark 1:2), joined to Isaiah 40:3. The two lines in Malachi, 'my messenger' and 'the messenger of the covenant', do not need to be two people. One reading takes them as one person who prepares and then is the coming Lord himself. Another keeps them apart: first the forerunner, then the Lord. Christians have applied the first to John and the second to Christ. Jewish tradition has applied the first to Elijah.

echoes: Exodus 23:20; Isaiah 40:3; Isaiah 1:25; Zechariah 1:3; Zechariah 13:9; Haggai 1:10-11; Nehemiah 10:37-39; Nehemiah 13:10-13; Deuteronomy 14:22-29; Deuteronomy 28:1-14; Psalm 103:13; Matthew 11:10; Mark 1:2; Luke 7:27

settings.what: The call to return and the test of the tithe
settings.to: The whole nation of Judah (3:9 says 'the whole nation of you'), above all the heads of households who owed the tithe and the contribution
settings.when: In the Persian period, in a time of poor harvests, crop pests and a Temple staff short of food (compare Nehemiah 13:10-13)
settings.why: To tell a community that says it has no idea how to return that the way is concrete: stop withholding the tithe and the contribution, bring all of it to the storehouse, and see the harvest answer. The speaker addresses a whole people, and the promise is material and for the community: rain and harvest in return for supporting a Temple that depended on them. The tithe fed the Levites and priests who could not own land.
settings.readers: The same first readers, the Judean community of the Persian period.
views: A call to a farming community
The blessing is rain and harvest, in the language of Deuteronomy 28.
A call to the Temple's support in particular
The storehouse and the Levites' shares are the problem Nehemiah 13 describes.

settings.what: The hard words, the scroll of remembrance and the day
settings.to: Two groups in the community: those who say it is pointless to serve God and call the proud happy, and those who fear the LORD and speak together
settings.when: In the Persian period, when the promises of Haggai and Zechariah (a glorious Temple, the nations' wealth, a restored king) had not come true
settings.why: To answer the doubt that service gets nothing back, by promising a day when the difference between the righteous and the wicked will be plain, and to encourage the small group of faithful that they are remembered. Knowing the setting shows a community sorting itself between disappointment and perseverance.
views: A message to a divided community
The doubters and the faithful are both Judeans, and the passage is meant to move the first to join the second.
A message for the faithful remnant
The doubters are the foil; the real audience is the small group of 3:16.

traditions.q: Is Christians' giving a tithe, and may Malachi 3:10 be read as a promise of return?
views: The Church's fifth precept is to provide for the needs of the Church according to one's ability (Catechism 2043; Code of Canon Law canon 222); the Old Testament tithe is a model of the offering, not a fixed rule.
No Orthodox canon or confession that I can cite fixes a tithe; giving is taught as part of stewardship and worship, and many parishes teach the tithe as a standard. Practice differs by jurisdiction.

The Reformed confessions do not settle it, and Reformed teachers divide: some call the tithe a standard that predates Moses (Genesis 14:20; Genesis 28:22) and still guides giving; others hold that it belonged to the temporary law of Israel and teach proportionate, cheerful giving (2 Corinthians 8-9).

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article XIV) says Christians should give cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately and liberally; many Baptist churches teach the tithe as the starting standard, while others call it an Old Testament rule.

Pentecostal bodies have no single rule. Many Pentecostal and charismatic churches teach the tithe as a duty and some link it to God's promised blessing; others in the movement reject the 'prosperity' use of Malachi 3:10 as a promise to individuals.

The tithe belongs to Israel's age under the law; in the church age, giving is a matter of grace and freewill (2 Corinthians 9:6-7), and Malachi 3:10 is a covenant promise to Israel, not a rule for the church.

title: The Day and Elijah
sum: The last chapter, which the Hebrew Bible counts as the end of chapter 3, speaks of the coming day. It burns like an oven, and the proud and the evildoers are stubble with no root and no branch. For those who fear the LORD's name, a sun of righteousness will rise, with healing in its wings, and they will go out and frisk like calves let out of the stall. They will trample the wicked, who will be ashes under their feet on the day when the LORD acts.

The book ends with two commands. Remember the law of Moses, given at Horeb for all Israel. And look: the LORD is sending Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day, to turn the hearts of fathers to sons and sons to fathers, or else the LORD will come and strike the land and put it under the ban. In the Christian Bible, the next page is Matthew.
readings: Read as a promise of justice

4:1-3 answers the people's doubt in 3:14-15: the proud who seemed to prosper are fuel, the faithful are healed. The picture is the day of the LORD, in two aspects: fire for the wicked and light for the righteous.
Read as an ending for the Twelve

4:4-6 may be an editor's closing for the Book of the Twelve or for the Prophets: it ties the prophets to the law of Moses and looks forward to Elijah, so the whole collection ends with a call and a warning.
Read as a hope that is open

The last words are not a promise of a new king or a new temple. They are a call to obey the old law and to wait for a messenger. Jewish and Christian readers have each read the open ending as pointing to their own hope.

views.H: In the Persian period the 'day' is the day when the LORD acts against the proud and for his faithful. Elijah, who did not die (2 Kings 2:11), is an obvious figure for a return. The reference to Horeb and 'rules and rulings' fits the interest of the age of Ezra and Nehemiah in the law of Moses (Nehemiah 8; Nehemiah 10:29).
views.C: Many critics think 4:4-6 is an addition by an editor who closed the Twelve, or the Prophets, with a reminder of the law and a hope in Elijah. The Greek puts the Moses verse last, the Hebrew first of the three closing verses; the Greek 'Elijah the Tishbite', 'will restore' and 'a person to his neighbor' read differently. The 'sun of righteousness' may borrow the winged sun image of the Persian world.
views.J: Jews end the public reading by repeating Hebrew 3:23 (English 4:5) after the last verse. The Mishnah says Elijah will come to make peace (Eduyot 8:7). The Talmud uses 4:1-3 for the sun that burns the wicked and heals the righteous (Avodah Zarah 3b). Malachi 3:4-24 (Hebrew) is the haftarah for Shabbat HaGadol before Passover, when a cup is set aside for Elijah in later custom.
views.X: Jesus says John is the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:10-13; Mark 9:11-13), and Luke has the angel say John will go before the Lord 'with Elijah's spirit and power' (Luke 1:17). The 'sun of righteousness' is a title of Christ for Jerome and Calvin, and the 'Dawn from on high' of Luke 1:78 echoes it. Malachi 4:1-2 is read in the lectionaries in the weeks before Advent. The cards show the churches' differences on Elijah.
views.F: Some readers hold that 4:5-6 awaits a final Elijah (or someone like him) before the future day of the LORD; they point to the two witnesses of Revelation 11, and to the fact that Jesus said 'Elijah is coming' as well as 'Elijah came already' (Matthew 17:11-12). Others hold that John was the full fulfillment of 4:5-6. Most of them keep the day of 4:1-3 as the end of the age, still ahead; preterist readers hold that the burning day came in the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70.

deep.h: The end of the Twelve, the Prophets and the Old Testament
deep.b: In the Hebrew Bible the Prophets end with the Twelve and the Twelve with Malachi; Chronicles stands last of the Writings. In the Christian Old Testament, where the books are grouped by kind, the Prophets come last and Malachi is the final book, so that the next page is Matthew. In the Greek manuscripts the Twelve stand at the start of the Prophets. These orders create different endings: for the Hebrew, a return to the law and a promised Elijah; for the Christian Bible, a coming messenger before the Gospel of the one who is announced. That the order creates meaning is a view of canon criticism (Childs). It is not a doctrine.

In Judaism, Elijah is the forerunner of the Messiah, the settler of disputes (Mishnah Eduyot 8:7) and the guest of the Passover table. In the New Testament, John is Elijah in spirit (Matthew 11:14; Luke 1:17), and the crowd at the cross misunderstands Jesus's cry as a call to Elijah (Matthew 27:47-49). At the Transfiguration Moses and Elijah, the law and the prophets, stand with Jesus (Matthew 17:3). The churches differ about whether the promise was fulfilled once, or is also still to come; see the card.

echoes: Joel 2:11; Joel 2:31; Obadiah 1:18; Deuteronomy 4:1-5; Deuteronomy 18:15; Deuteronomy 34:10-12; 1 Kings 19:8; 2 Kings 2:11; Isaiah 58:8; Psalm 84:11; Sirach 48:10; Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:10-13; Mark 9:11-13; Luke 1:17; Luke 1:78; John 1:21

settings.what: The closing command and the promise of Elijah
settings.by: The LORD, through Malachi (or an editor who closed the book)
settings.to: All Israel, in the words 'for all Israel' (4:4), the whole community of the Persian period and the later readers of the Twelve and the Prophets
settings.when: At the end of the book. Many scholars date it later than the disputes, as an editorial close
settings.why: To give a community still waiting for justice something to do and something to hope for: remember the law of Moses (keep the covenant), and expect a messenger who will turn the generations to each other before the great day. Knowing it closes the Prophets shows that it joins them to the Law and looks beyond them.
settings.readers: Readers of the Twelve and the Prophets, who would hear the last words as the closing of a collection.
views: The verses answer the book's questions about the day and the priests' teaching.
The verses were added to close the Twelve, or the Prophets, with Moses and Elijah (Childs, Nogalski).

traditions.q: Was Elijah's coming in Malachi 4:5-6 fulfilled in John the Baptist, or is it still to come?
views: John fulfilled the promise 'in the spirit and power of Elijah' (Luke 1:17; Catechism 718, 719), and the Catechism calls him the 'forerunner' of the Lord. The Catholic tradition also holds an old expectation that Elijah himself will return before the end (Augustine, City of God 20.29, expects him to turn the Jews to Christ before the judgment); the Catechism passages speak of John because they are about John, not because they deny a final Elijah.
John the Forerunner is the Elijah of Malachi (Matthew 11:14), and the Orthodox also honor the old Christian expectation, found in several fathers, that Elijah himself will come before the end.
Calvin held that Malachi spoke of John, who came in Elijah's spirit and power, and not of a literal return of Elijah; John's own 'I am not' (John 1:21) means he was not Elijah in person.

Some hold that Elijah, or one in his spirit, will appear before the future day of the LORD, since Malachi's great and awesome day has not yet come, and often identify him with one of the two witnesses of Revelation 11; others in the movement see John as the fulfillment.

Elijah appeared in the Kirtland Temple in 1836 and restored the sealing power that turns hearts of children and fathers to each other, which fulfills Malachi 4:5-6 (Doctrine and Covenants 110:13-16; 2:1-3).
